name: Maya Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the disability benefits team at the regional office near the bus station. Most of my day is reading medical evidence, GP letters and care plans, then ringing claimants to fill the gaps before I write up a decision. I like the calls, because people tell you things the forms never ask about. What wears me down is writing the same reasons paragraph forty times a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The office rolled out a summary tool last year, and I use it for long hospital reports once I've seen others trust it. I still check everything, because I caught it calling a wheelchair user 'mobile' once. My partner Tomás teaches Year 4 and thinks I worry too much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, it's a better spellchecker and that's that. At work I'd probably joke that the summary tool finally earned its keep on hospital letters. Online I wouldn't bother saying much, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite pleased. My job stays, my pay's good for this kind of work, and there are other benefits offices across the city if I ever want a change. I'd still want the reasons paragraph automated, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the summary tool on long reports. Tomás and I would carry on saving for a wedding next summer, about 8,000 set aside already. I'd probably apply for the senior caseworker post when it opens in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the idea, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The backlog. We're at eleven weeks to a decision, and people are waiting on rent and food while we read their files. AI being hype doesn't fix that, more staff would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for more staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the union petition and go to the branch meeting, sure. I'm not the person who organises it, but I turn up.

say: I'd say AI is just a **better spellchecker** and leave it there.
I'd joke at work that the **summary tool** finally earned its keep on hospital letters.
think: My **job and pay** stay solid, with other benefits offices across the city if needed.
The real problem stays the **eleven-week backlog**, which only more staff would fix.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** on long hospital reports, checking every line.
Apply for the **senior caseworker** post when it opens in spring.
Keep saving for the **wedding** with Tomás next summer.
feel: **Calm**, a little bored by the idea, but settled.
S0.quote: We're at eleven weeks to a decision, and people are waiting on rent and food while we read their files.
fieldNote: Maya is **secure** and knows it, with savings and a city full of similar offices.
Her frustration is the **backlog**, not technology.
She is a **joiner**, not an organiser, of union action.

steps.text: Use the summary tool on long hospital reports and check each line
Apply for the senior caseworker post in spring
Sign the union petition for more disability team staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we have to make sure a person still signs every disability decision. I'd probably share posts from disability charities saying the same thing. I'd want to sound reasonable, not like I'm against all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my team shrinks. Reading evidence, writing reasons and answering calls are exactly the thinking tasks on that card. I think they'd keep a few of us to sign off, and I'm average, not the best, so I can't count on being one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly in the first six months, once the early people have worked out the bugs. I'd look at moving into the appeals team, where you still sit in tribunal hearings with people. I'd also keep 15,000 of savings untouched, and maybe push the wedding to a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. I'd sleep fine, but I'd feel it every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to sound reasonable. What's the less reasonable thing you'd want to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Letting software decide whether someone with MS can pay their heating would be a disgrace. I'd think that, but I'd say it more politely at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomás say if you suggested a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás (my partner) would say he never wanted the big one anyway. My mum would be the one upset, because she's already booked the hall in her head.

say: I'd say a **person** must still sign every disability decision.
I'd share **disability charity** posts making the same case, keeping my tone reasonable.
think: Reading evidence and writing reasons are exactly the **tasks** AI takes first.
I'm **average**, so I can't count on being one of the few kept to sign off.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly in the first six months, once bugs are fixed.
Ask to move into the **appeals team**, where hearings still need people.
Keep **15,000** untouched and scale the wedding down.
feel: **Anxious** in a quiet way that shows up every Monday morning.
S1.quote: Letting software decide whether someone with MS can pay their heating would be a disgrace.
fieldNote: Her **public tone** is softer than her private view.
She waits for others before adopting tools, then **commits**.
The **appeals team** is her chosen shelter because it involves people in rooms.

steps.text: Take the new caseworking system training within six months
Apply for a transfer to the appeals team
Book a smaller wedding venue instead of the big hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and the government needs to protect people first, including its own workers. I'd go to whatever rally the union and the disability groups organised. Online I'd be much louder than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of work by 2028 or soon after. My job is nearly all screen and phone work, so there's no three-year buffer for me. The only part that's hands-on is the odd home visit, and that's not enough to build a job on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding in the first month and sit down with Tomás to go through the money. We'd keep the savings for rent and live on his salary as much as we can. I'd start looking at teaching, like him, or care work, because those are hands-on with people and the robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly frightened, the kind where you can't concentrate on the telly at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the wedding is still happening, just not next summer. I'd tell her I need to find a new job before everyone else does. She'd say something about how my grandmother cleaned offices and was never out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Tomás's job feel safe to you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot can't calm thirty eight-year-olds after lunch yet, so Tomás (my partner) is safer than me for three years at least. But I'd worry the lesson planning goes on day one.

say: I'd call it a **public emergency** and demand the government protect people first.
I'd join any **rally** organised by the union and disability groups.
think: I'm likely **out of work** by 2028, with no three-year buffer.
My only hands-on part is the odd **home visit**, which can't carry a job.
do: Postpone the **wedding** in the first month and go through the money with Tomás.
Live on Tomás's **salary** where possible and protect savings for rent.
Look into **teaching or care work** to use the three-year robot gap.
feel: **Frightened** enough that she can't concentrate in the evenings.
S2.quote: A robot can't calm thirty eight-year-olds after lunch yet, so Tomás (my partner) is safer than me for three years at least.
fieldNote: She reads her job as almost entirely **thinking work** and sees no buffer.
The **wedding** becomes the first visible casualty.
Her household rests on Tomás's **hands-on** job, which she also doubts.
Family memory of a **cleaner grandmother** comes up as a quiet reproach.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding until after the job change
Apply for a teaching assistant or care role before 2028
Join union and disability group rallies for worker protection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, I'd say we need protections, but I'd be calmer about it. I'd tell colleagues to use the time to train for something else. Online I'd share stuff about transition funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job still ends around 2031. Five years means I could finish a proper qualification first, not just grab any job. That's the real difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time teaching qualification in the first year, probably the primary route, evenings and weekends. I'd keep working full time and saving. We'd have the wedding as planned, but smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It feels like a deadline more than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to fit in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Thursday netball and probably most weekends for two years. Tomás would end up doing all the cooking, which he'd complain about and secretly enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching rather than something like appeals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Appeals is still thinking work, and in this picture thinking work goes in 2031, so I'd rather train for a classroom. Teaching has a classroom and actual children, so I'd get until about 2034, and maybe longer.

say: I'd call for **protections** but tell colleagues to use the time to train.
I'd share posts online about **transition funds** for public workers.
think: My job still ends around **2031**, but now I can plan.
Five years lets me finish a **proper qualification** instead of grabbing any job.
do: Start a **part-time teaching** qualification in the first year.
Keep working **full time** and keep saving throughout the course.
Hold a **smaller wedding** on the planned date.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, more like a **deadline** than a cliff.
S3.quote: Appeals is still thinking work, and in this picture thinking work goes in 2031, so I'd rather train for a classroom.
fieldNote: She uses the robot gap **deliberately** to pick teaching over appeals.
Time turns her fear into a **study plan**.
Hobbies like **netball** are what she'd sacrifice first.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time primary teaching qualification
Keep working full time at the disability team while studying
Hold a smaller wedding on the planned date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so the government has no excuse not to plan it properly. At work I'd encourage people to start thinking about their next step. I wouldn't be dramatic about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'd have the senior caseworker job for a few years, then shift. I'd be 37 when the thinking work goes, so young enough. My worry is more about Tomás, because 2039 isn't that far away for a teacher either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the senior post next year and save hard while the pay is good. Around year four I'd train in something people-facing, maybe teaching, maybe social work. Tomás and I would have the wedding next summer as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sharply. It's background noise, not a siren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra money from the senior post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it toward a house deposit, honestly. If both our jobs go eventually, I'd rather own the roof than rent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not writing the reasons paragraph again, ever. If AI did that in year one, I'd have more time on the phone with people, which is the bit I like.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so government has **no excuse** for a bad plan.
I'd encourage colleagues to think about their **next step** early.
think: I'd hold the **senior post** a few years, then shift at about 37.
My bigger worry is **Tomás**, because 2039 isn't far off for teachers either.
do: Apply for the **senior caseworker** post next year and save the extra pay.
Train in **teaching or social work** around year four.
Put savings toward a **house deposit** with Tomás.
feel: **Anxious** as background noise rather than a siren.
S4.quote: If both our jobs go eventually, I'd rather own the roof than rent it.
fieldNote: The long runway lets her **climb** before she switches.
She expects both household jobs to be hit, so the **house** is her hedge.
She'd **welcome** losing the repetitive writing parts.

steps.text: Apply for the senior caseworker post next year
Put the senior post's extra pay into a house deposit
Start teaching or social work training around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it lands before I could finish any course and it hits Tomás too, three years later. What would help is paid time off to retrain and an income that bridges the gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the claimants. Every scenario where my job goes is one where the people I help are waiting on a system nobody can phone.

headlineQuote: Every scenario where my job goes is one where the people I help are waiting on a system nobody can phone.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** disability benefits caseworker who uses AI summaries now and then.
She feels **secure** if AI stalls, and expects her team to shrink under steady disruption.
Her plan is to move toward **teaching** or social work, timed to the robot gap.
Her partner Tomás and a planned **wedding** shape most of her choices.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands before she could finish retraining and hits Tomás later.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** time and an income that bridges the gap between jobs.
